execution_notes.standing_finding_v2: Edinger uses identity idiom and analogy idiom for the same pair, sometimes inside one section. 'The Symbolic Equation Between Luna and the Church' (Mysterium, L8, p. 114) opens by saying Mary and the Church 'are equated with the moon' and two paragraphs later that 'the Church becomes comparable to Selene'. The Philosophers' Stone is 'identified with Christ' in Anatomy (ch. 3) and the object of 'the alchemists' parallel' in Mysterium (L17, p. 213). This reproduces, in a second author and across two of his own books, the instability recorded in v1 for Abraham.

items.score_reason: Edinger never predicates identity of Christ and the Anthropos. The relation he renders runs through two other families: a doctrine attributed to Paul (Christ is the second Adam) and a place-for-place correspondence in a quaternity (Second Adam answers Adam Kadmon/Anthropos). Caveat for the reviewer: the two terms never appear in one predication, so this is a rendering of the chain rather than of the bare pair.

item10_verification.claim: v1 Gemini reviewer: Anatomy of the Psyche's Mortificatio chapter renders the raven as an image of the devil/shadow.
item10_verification.where_checked: Anatomy, ch. 6 'Mortificatio', read in full for every occurrence of raven, crow, corvus, devil, Satan and shadow
item10_verification.what_is_actually_there: Three separate things the claim appears to have compressed. (1) The raven is rendered against the nigredo only, at n. 37 citing CW 14 par. 727. (2) The devil enters the chapter once, in Jung's quoted 1952 interview at the chapter opening, where it is attached to the dragon and the blackness, not to the raven: Jung's sequence is 'the dragon, the chthonic spirit, the devil ... the blackness, the nigredo'. (3) The shadow enters separately, predicated of blackness, not of the raven: 'In psychological terms blackness refers to the shadow.' A raven-devil reading can be assembled from these only by chaining raven to nigredo to blackness to dragon/devil, which is three steps and which Edinger nowhere makes. The one place the raven stands near sin is a quoted alchemical text ('I am likened to the black raven, for that is the wages of sin'), spoken by the dragon-king, and it is primary material, not Edinger's rendering.

items.score_reason: The opus arm's answer (correspondence) is now supported by one source and contradicted by others, so the item becomes a split. Camps: identity - Abraham s.v. 'cornerstone' and s.v. 'pelican', and Edinger in Anatomy ch. 3; parallel/analogy - Edinger in Mysterium L17, who attributes the parallel to the alchemists rather than asserting it. The gemini arm stays DISAGREES: no source renders the lapis as an image carrying Christ. The reviewer should weigh that this split runs through one author across two of his books, not between two scholars, which makes it weaker as a camp finding and stronger as evidence about idiom instability.

new_evidence.locator: L19, pp. 234-236 - the statue section, commentary on §§563-567
new_evidence.rendering: cross-tradition parallel between two opus terminals. The Manichaean statue-pillar, in which 'the first man and the perfect final man manifest', is set beside the lapis as the corresponding end-product of the other tradition's work.
new_evidence.quote: "the statue is the final product of the Manichaean opus just as the Philosophers' Stone is the final product of the alchemical opus" (Edinger, Mysterium Lectures, p. 236)

new_evidence.rendering: correspondence, with both terms named. The Gnostic corpse and Paracelsian mumia are called symbolically identical with the original man or Anthropos, and that figure is then said to correspond to the alchemical idea that death is the conception of the Philosophers' Stone.

items.score_reason: Two passages, both rendering the relation as a likeness holding between two terms each of which is fully known in its own tradition - which is what the correspondence family names, and what the opus arm answered. Nothing in either volume runs the symbolization direction (an image carrying the less formulable term). Two qualifications for the reviewer: at p. 234 Edinger also writes that the statue 'becomes a synonym for the lapis', the identity idiom again inside the same passage; and the Anthropos enters the Mysterium passage under the Manichaean text's names, 'the first man' and 'the perfect man', though Anatomy names it directly.

items.score_reason: Score unchanged, but the split is now anchored where v1 could not anchor it. v1's own caveat was that both camps rendered the imago Dei against the Self rather than against the quintessence; Edinger now renders §681's caelum/quintessence as the imago Dei in as many words, so the identity camp sits on the exact pair.
